extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proofs / introductory discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook section introducing indexed sets, unions/intersections (finite and infinite), basic number-system set facts (well-ordering, division algorithm, set-constructions, Russell's paradox) and the foundations of propositional logic (statements, open sentences, ∧, ∨, ∼, ⇒) with definitions, examples, and truth tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of finitely many sets (Definition 1.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given sets A1, A2, ..., An, A1 ∪ A2 ∪ ... ∪ An = { x : x ∈ Ai for at least one set Ai, for 1 ≤ i ≤ n }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains membership criterion: an element is in the union iff it belongs to at least one of the constituent sets; examples given (Example 1.12) show computing unions for concrete finite sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection of finitely many sets (Definition 1.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given sets A1, A2, ..., An, A1 ∩ A2 ∩ ... ∩ An = { x : x ∈ Ai for every set Ai, for 1 ≤ i ≤ n }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains membership criterion: an element is in the intersection iff it belongs to every set; examples (Example 1.12) illustrate computing intersections for concrete finite sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sigma-like notation for unions and intersections
rubrics_metrics.description: Notation analogous to sigma sums: ∪_{i=1}^n A_i = A1 ∪ ... ∪ An and ∩_{i=1}^n A_i = A1 ∩ ... ∩ An; extends to infinite lists ∪_{i=1}^∞ A_i and ∩_{i=1}^∞ A_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that this compact notation handles large or infinite collections; examples include both finite (n=3) and infinite lists (Example 1.13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexed sets and index sets
rubrics_metrics.description: When many sets are involved, use subscripts (A1, A2, ...) or more generally A_α for α in an index set I; I is the set of possible subscripts and need not be integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates switching to α (not i) for general index elements; clarifies that index sets can be arbitrary (e.g., real intervals) and gives geometric examples (Example 1.14 where I = [0,2]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Union and intersection over an index set I (Definition 1.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a collection {A_α : α ∈ I}, ∪_{α∈I} A_α = { x : x ∈ A_α for at least one α ∈ I } and ∩_{α∈I} A_α = { x : x ∈ A_α for every α ∈ I }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies whether I is finite, countably infinite, or uncountable; examples include unions/intersections over continuous index sets producing geometric figures (triangles, axes, whole space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-integer indexing (illustrative examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Index sets can be non-integer (e.g., real interval I = [0,2]); A_α can be defined for each real α producing a continuum of sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show how ∪_{α∈[0,2]} A_α and ∩_{α∈[0,2]} A_α produce specific geometric regions (shaded triangle, single point), illustrating subtle membership logic for uncountable index sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number systems as sets and accepted algebraic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Common number systems (N, Z, Q, R) are treated as sets whose elements can be added/multiplied and whose operations satisfy familiar algebraic properties (commutative, associative, distributive) and ordering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties are accepted as ground rules and not proved in detail in this chapter; the text warns that some consequences (e.g., well-ordering for N) will be used freely in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-ordering principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Any non-empty subset of the positive integers N has a smallest element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principle is used often in proofs (often without comment); it is noted to be false for the positive real numbers and is linked to fundamental facts like the division algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division Algorithm (Fact 1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given integers a and b with b > 0, there exist unique integers q and r for which a = q b + r and 0 ≤ r < b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch of proof given using the well-ordering principle: form the set of nonnegative integers a - x b and take its least element r; shows existence and explains why r < b; uniqueness left to an exercise reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-theoretic construction of natural numbers (Von Neumann style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural numbers can be modeled as sets: 0 = ∅, 1 = {0}, 2 = {0,1}, 3 = {0,1,2}, and generally n = {0,1,...,n−1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes this is possible and that even operations can be defined set-theoretically, but the book will not undertake the full study—this supports the remark that mathematics can be described in terms of sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Russell's paradox and the set A = { X : X is a set and X ∉ X }
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing A leads to the question 'Is A ∈ A?' which yields a contradiction (A ∈ A iff A ∉ A), illustrating a paradox arising from naive set comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides illustrative examples (e.g., the nested self-containing B = {B}) and explains that this paradox motivated axiomatic set theory (Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms) to avoid such contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom of foundation (informal statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: One Zermelo-Fraenkel axiom: no non-empty set X is allowed to have the property X ∩ x ≠ ∅ for all its elements x (rules out circularly defined/self-containing sets like B = {B}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that adopting such axioms removes paradoxes like Russell's; notes that most mathematicians accept these axioms and that paradoxes rarely arise in everyday mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a statement (Section 2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement is a sentence or a mathematical expression that is either definitely true or definitely false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes statements are the basic units to which logic is applied; examples of true and false statements are given and the distinction between correct logic vs correct information is discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open sentences and variables
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence containing variables whose truth depends on the values of the variables (e.g., Q(x): 'x is even') is called an open sentence and is not a statement until variables are specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation P(x), P(x,y) is used to emphasize dependence on variables; open sentences can become statements when variables are instantiated or quantified (quantifiers discussed later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of propositional letters (P, Q, R) as shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters P, Q, R, S (with subscripts if needed) denote specific statements or open sentences for convenience in symbolic reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shorthand simplifies repeated reference to complex sentences and is standard practice in proofs and logic exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunction (and, ∧) and its truth table
rubrics_metrics.description: For statements P and Q, P ∧ Q asserts both P and Q are true; truth table: T∧T = T; T∧F = F; F∧T = F; F∧F = F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains membership/validity: conjunction is true only when both components are true; examples provided (e.g., '2 is even and 3 is odd').

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjunction (or, ∨) as inclusive or and its truth table
rubrics_metrics.description: For statements P and Q, P ∨ Q means one or both of P and Q is true (inclusive); truth table: T∨T = T; T∨F = T; F∨T = T; F∨F = F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes difference from everyday exclusive 'or' and gives constructions to express 'exactly one' (e.g., 'P or Q, but not both'); provides examples illustrating inclusive vs exclusive usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation (not, ∼) and its truth table
rubrics_metrics.description: For a statement P, ∼P (not P) is true exactly when P is false and false when P is true; truth table: P=T => ∼P=F; P=F => ∼P=T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives multiple equivalent phrasings for a negation (e.g., 'It's not true that...', 'The number 2 is not even') and demonstrates usage with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional statements (if P then Q, ⇒) and their truth table/interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: P ⇒ Q (If P then Q) means whenever P is true, Q must also be true; truth table: T⇒T = T; T⇒F = F; F⇒T = T; F⇒F = T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprets ⇒ as a promise that can only be falsified by P true and Q false; gives everyday and mathematical examples (professor promise, equinox/month), and lists many equivalent phrasings ('P implies Q', 'Q whenever P', 'P is a sufficient condition for Q', 'P only if Q', etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between correct logic and correct information
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is the process of deducing information correctly; conclusions can be logically correct even when premises (information) are false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If premises assert radius 3 then area 9π follows by correct logic even if, in fact, the radius were 4; emphasizes importance of both correct logic and correct premises in proofs.
